before.flash_fill_tip: Type the cleaned version of 2–3 cells manually, then press Ctrl + E. Excel detects the pattern and applies it to the entire column. It's not a function (no formula is created), so use it for quick one-time cleaning, not for dynamic models.

after.flash_fill_tip: Type the cleaned version of 2–3 cells manually, then press Ctrl + E. Excel detects the pattern and applies it to the entire column. It's not a function (no formula is created), so use it for quick one-time cleaning, not for dynamic models.

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to extract from
Number of characters to extract from the left (optional, defaults to 1)

functions_table.plain_english: Extracts the first n characters from the beginning of a text string. Useful for isolating prefixes, like extracting a company code from a ticker symbol or the first few characters of a product name for classification.

functions_table.note: Combine with LEN for dynamic extraction

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to extract from
Number of characters to extract from the right

functions_table.plain_english: Extracts the last n characters from the end of a text string. Common in finance for pulling suffixes like fiscal year indicators (e.g., last 2 digits of 'FY2024' to get '24') or the right-most digits of an identifier.

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to extract from
Position of the first character to extract (1-indexed, where 1 is the first character)
Number of characters to extract

functions_table.plain_english: Extracts a substring of length n starting at position start. Useful for pulling out middle segments, such as extracting quarter codes from date formats or isolating segments of a multi-part identifier (e.g., 'Q3' from 'FY2024Q3').

functions_table.note: Includes spaces; compare with TRIM to find extras

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to measure

functions_table.plain_english: Counts the total number of characters in a text string, including spaces and punctuation. Use to identify data quality issues (unexpected lengths) or to validate that text entries conform to a standard format.

functions_table.note: Removes leading, trailing, and extra internal spaces

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to clean

functions_table.plain_english: Removes all leading and trailing spaces, and reduces multiple internal spaces to single spaces. Essential for cleaning imported data before performing matches or concatenations, especially common when data comes from PDFs or poorly formatted sources.

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to clean

functions_table.plain_english: Removes non-printable characters (like hidden line breaks and special encoding artifacts) from text. Combine with TRIM for comprehensive cleaning when importing data from legacy systems or web sources.

variables.meaning: The original text string or cell reference
The substring to find and replace (case-sensitive)
The replacement text

functions_table.plain_english: Finds and replaces all (or a specific instance of) a substring with new text. Useful for standardising company names, converting ticker symbols, or replacing abbreviations (e.g., changing 'Ltd.' to 'Limited' across a column).

variables.meaning: Text values or cell references to join together

functions_table.plain_english: Joins multiple text strings into one. Modern Excel prefers the & operator (e.g., A1 & B1) for brevity, but CONCATENATE is still useful when joining many values programmatically.

variables.meaning: The delimiter character(s) to insert between joined values (e.g., ', ' or '; ')
Boolean: TRUE to skip empty cells, FALSE to include them
The range of cells to join

functions_table.plain_english: Joins a range of cells with a specified delimiter, optionally skipping empty cells. Powerful for consolidating lists (e.g., combining multiple analyst names into a single 'Research Team' field) without manual concatenation.

functions_table.note: Use before MATCH for case-insensitive lookups

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to convert

functions_table.plain_english: Converts all letters to uppercase. Useful for standardising company names or ticker symbols before comparison, ensuring that lookups are case-insensitive.

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to convert

functions_table.plain_english: Converts all letters to lowercase. Use for data standardisation before performing string comparisons or lookups, especially when integrating data from sources with inconsistent casing.

functions_table.note: Capitalises first letter of every word

variables.meaning: The text string or cell reference to convert

functions_table.plain_english: Converts text to title case (first letter of each word capitalised, rest lowercase). Ideal for cleaning company names and analyst names for professional report formatting.

functions_table.note: Loses numeric properties — for display only

variables.meaning: The numeric value or date to format
A format code string (e.g., '₹#,##0.00' for Indian currency, 'dd-mmm-yyyy' for dates)

functions_table.plain_english: Converts a number or date into formatted text according to a specified format code. Useful for displaying numbers as currency (₹), percentages, or dates in a specific locale format. The result is text, not a number, so use only for display or export.

worked_example.problem: You have a revenue value of 12500000 (₹1.25 crore) and need to display it as formatted text for a report: ₹1,25,00,000.
steps: Excel applies the Indian numbering format (groups of two after the initial three digits)
Result: ₹1,25,00,000 — text format suitable for export or display
worked_example.insight: TEXT is purely for display. If you need to use the formatted number in calculations afterward, convert it back to a number with VALUE(). Always use TEXT near the end of a model, not during intermediate calculations.

functions_table.note: Use after SUBSTITUTE to convert text-numbers

variables.meaning: A text string representing a number, possibly including currency symbols or thousands separators

functions_table.plain_english: Converts a text string that represents a number back into a numeric value. Essential after importing formatted text (e.g., '₹1,25,00,000' or '50%') so you can use it in calculations.

variables.meaning: The substring to locate (case-sensitive)
The text string or cell reference to search within
Optional starting position for the search (defaults to 1)

functions_table.plain_english: Returns the position (1-indexed) of the first occurrence of a substring, with case sensitivity. Use FIND when you need exact case matching (e.g., distinguishing 'Rs' from 'rs'), or combine with IFERROR to handle missing values gracefully.

variables.meaning: The substring or pattern to locate (case-insensitive; supports * and ? wildcards)
The text string or cell reference to search within
Optional starting position for the search (defaults to 1)

functions_table.plain_english: Returns the position of the first occurrence of a substring, ignoring case. Unlike FIND, SEARCH supports wildcards (* for any characters, ? for a single character), making it more flexible for pattern matching. Use when case doesn't matter or you need fuzzy matching.
